$description: Applicability rules. Declarative data evaluated by a deliberately unintelligent matcher: a rule fires when every dimension it specifies intersects the user's selection, and a dimension the rule omits is a wildcard. There is no decision tree in the JavaScript — the reasoning lives here and is inspectable.

$outcomes.outcome:applies: Likely applies — on the facts given, a rule for the instrument fires. A case-specific assessment is still required.
$outcomes.outcome:likely: Potentially applicable — applies on the ordinary reading, but turns on a condition not established here.
$outcomes.outcome:possible: Potentially applicable — may apply, depending on facts this questionnaire does not ask for.
$outcomes.outcome:unlikely: Likely not applicable — but absence of an obligation here is not a safe harbour.
$outcomes.outcome:undetermined: NOT A RULE OUTCOME. Emitted by the engine when no rule covers the combination. Absence of a rule is absence of knowledge, never evidence of non-applicability.

$limits: This is a map of the rulebook, not legal advice, and cannot be. It asks three questions where a lawyer would ask fifty.
Every rule is drawn from the brief's own analysis and the instruments cited in it. Coverage is uneven by design: the six core instruments are covered in depth, the adjacent ones barely.
A threshold the questionnaire does not establish downgrades an outcome by one step rather than excluding the rule, so a borderline case is shown rather than hidden.
Sectoral, national and contractual obligations are almost entirely outside this dataset. A clean result here says nothing about them.

rules.rationale: Any processing of personal data by a controller or processor established in the Union falls within the GDPR, whatever the sector and whatever the size of the organisation. There is no de minimis exemption from the Regulation as a whole.

exemptions.text: Purely personal or household activity is outside scope.

Under Article 30(5), an enterprise or organisation employing fewer than 250 persons need not keep records of processing activities, unless its processing is likely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects, is not occasional, or includes special categories of data or personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences.

rules.rationale: Article 3(2) reaches a controller not established in the Union where the processing relates to offering goods or services to data subjects in the Union, or to monitoring their behaviour. Whether either limb is met is a question of fact about targeting that this questionnaire does not establish — merely being accessible from the Union is not enough.
depends_on: Whether the offering is directed at data subjects in the Union, or their behaviour is monitored.

rules.rationale: A public authority processing personal data owes the full obligation set, and must designate a data protection officer under Article 37 irrespective of the scale of processing.

exemptions.text: Processing by competent authorities for law-enforcement purposes falls under the Law Enforcement Directive rather than the GDPR — an instrument outside this dataset.
Processing by the Union's own institutions, bodies, offices and agencies is governed by a separate Union regulation rather than the GDPR — an instrument outside this dataset.
Courts acting in their judicial capacity are excepted from the obligation to designate a data protection officer that Article 37(1)(a) places on public authorities and bodies.

rules.rationale: Article 22 has governed decisions based solely on automated processing since 2018 and applies to systems the AI Act classifies as minimal risk. An AI system that produces legal or similarly significant effects for individuals engages it regardless of the AI Act tier the system falls into.
depends_on: Whether the system processes personal data at all.

rules.rationale: Obligations stack cumulatively across four tiers. An online platform owes the intermediary and hosting duties below it as well as the platform tier: notice and action, statements of reasons, internal complaint handling, the dark-pattern ban, advertising transparency and recommender-parameter disclosure.

exemptions.text: Under Article 19, providers of online platforms that are micro or small enterprises — and, for twelve months after losing that status, those that were — are exempt from the Section 3 online-platform obligations, except Article 24(3), unless designated as a very large online platform.

rules.rationale: A platform allowing consumers to conclude distance contracts with traders must obtain and check specified trader information before allowing use of the service, and must design its interface so that the trader's identity is visible.

exemptions.text: Under Article 29, providers of online platforms allowing consumers to conclude distance contracts with traders that are micro or small enterprises — and, for twelve months after losing that status, those that were — are exempt from the Section 4 marketplace obligations, unless designated as a very large online platform.

rules.rationale: Article 40 gives researchers a route to platform data rather than an obligation. Access to non-public data runs through the Digital Services Coordinator of establishment, not the platform, and is purpose-limited to the detection and understanding of systemic risks. The brief records that route as underperforming in practice.

exemptions.text: Article 40 reaches only VLOPs and VLOSEs. Smaller platforms are outside it entirely.

depends_on: Vetting by a Digital Services Coordinator.

rules.rationale: Every provider of a general-purpose AI model owes Article 53 since 2 August 2025: Annex XI technical documentation, an Annex XII information pack for downstream providers, a copyright compliance policy and a sufficiently detailed public summary of training content. The operative detail sits in the Code of Practice, which is voluntary.

exemptions.text: Article 53(2) partially exempts models released under a genuinely free and open-source licence — but the exemption evaporates entirely for systemic-risk models.

rules.rationale: The Chapter III high-risk obligations — risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logging, human oversight, accuracy and cybersecurity, conformity assessment and registration — reach a system only through one of the two Article 6 entry routes. Most deployed AI never leaves the minimal-risk tier. Following the AI Omnibus these duties arrive on 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for product-embedded ones.

exemptions.text: Under Article 6(3), an Annex III system that does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons, and meets one of the four conditions the paragraph lists, is not high-risk — never one that performs profiling of natural persons; the provider must document that assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service, and register it (Article 6(4)).

depends_on: Whether the system is a safety component of a product covered by Annex I harmonisation legislation.
Whether it falls within an Annex III use case — biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services, law enforcement, migration, or justice and democratic processes.

rules.rationale: The Article 5 prohibitions bind public authorities as well as firms. Social scoring by government, predictive policing based solely on profiling, and emotion recognition in workplaces and educational institutions are prohibited outright. Real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement is prohibited subject to narrow exceptions.

exemptions.text: Article 4(2) TEU reserves national security to the Member States, and the AI Act does not apply to systems placed on the market, put into service or used exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes (Art. 2(3)). The brief argues this carve-out is the structural source of the asymmetry between constraint on corporate and on state power.

depends_on: Whether the use is characterised as national security, which the Act does not itself resolve.

rules.rationale: Chapter VI is nine articles (Arts. 23-31) out of fifty and carries most of the Regulation's practical weight for the software industry. Providers of data processing services must remove all pre-commercial, commercial, technical, contractual and organisational obstacles to switching, and Article 25 prescribes the mandatory contractual terms.

exemptions.text: Under Article 31(2), the obligations of Chapter VI do not apply to data processing services provided as a non-production version for testing and evaluation purposes and for a limited period of time. Under Article 31(1), Article 29 does not apply — nor do Article 23, point (d), and Article 30(1) and (3) — to data processing services the majority of whose main features has been custom-built for an individual customer, or all of whose components have been developed for one, where they are not offered at broad commercial scale via the provider's service catalogue. The provider must inform the prospective customer beforehand of the obligations that do not apply (Article 31(3)).

depends_on: Whether Chapter VI reaches contracts concluded before 12 September 2025: Article 50 phases in only Chapter IV for such contracts, and practitioner analysis reads the switching right as reaching them; the Commission's FAQ (version 1.4) does not address the point.

exemptions.text: Under Article 31(2), the obligations of Chapter VI do not apply to data processing services provided as a non-production version for testing and evaluation purposes and for a limited period of time. The provider must inform the prospective customer beforehand of the obligations that do not apply (Article 31(3)).

rules.rationale: From 12 September 2026 connected products must be designed and manufactured so that product and related service data are, by default, easily, securely and directly accessible to the user. This is a design obligation, not a disclosure one: it bites at the point the product is placed on the market.

exemptions.text: Under Article 4(6) to (8), trade secrets are disclosed only where the data holder and the user take the measures necessary to preserve their confidentiality. Where no such measures are agreed, or the user fails to implement them or undermines that confidentiality, the data holder may withhold or suspend the sharing of data identified as trade secrets; in exceptional circumstances, where it can demonstrate that it is highly likely to suffer serious economic damage, it may refuse access case by case. In each case it must notify the competent authority, and the user may lodge a complaint with that authority or, by agreement with the data holder, refer the matter to a dispute settlement body, without prejudice to recourse to a court (Article 4(9)).

Under Article 7(1), the obligations of Chapter II, Article 3(1) among them, do not apply to data generated through the use of connected products manufactured or designed, or related services provided, by a microenterprise or a small enterprise that has no partner or linked enterprise which is not itself micro or small, and that is not subcontracted to manufacture or design the product or provide the service. The same applies to an enterprise that has qualified as medium-sized for less than one year, and to connected products for one year after a medium-sized enterprise placed them on the market.

rules.rationale: The Data Act governs product and service data as such — personal or not, though predominantly non-personal, industrial and machine-generated, with the GDPR prevailing wherever personal data is involved — and reallocates control over it by default. An organisation may be a data holder, a user or a data recipient depending on the arrangement, and the obligations differ in each role.

exemptions.text: Under Article 7(1), the obligations of Chapter II, Article 3(1) among them, do not apply to data generated through the use of connected products manufactured or designed, or related services provided, by a microenterprise or a small enterprise that has no partner or linked enterprise which is not itself micro or small, and that is not subcontracted to manufacture or design the product or provide the service. The same applies to an enterprise that has qualified as medium-sized for less than one year, and to connected products for one year after a medium-sized enterprise placed them on the market.

depends_on: Which role the organisation occupies: data holder, user, or data recipient.

rules.rationale: NIS2 sets ten baseline risk-management measures and a reporting cascade of 24 hours, 72 hours and one month. Article 20 makes management bodies approve and oversee the measures and liable for the entity's infringements, and Article 32(6) adds personal liability for those responsible at essential entities — the provision that actually changes boardroom behaviour. Whether an organisation is an essential or an important entity turns on its sector and size.
depends_on: THE OPERATIVE DATE IS NATIONAL, NOT EUROPEAN. NIS2 is a directive and transposition is materially incomplete: registration windows and compliance dates vary by Member State, and in several they have not yet arrived.

rules.rationale: Cloud computing service providers and data centre service providers sit within the digital infrastructure sector, which NIS2 treats as essential. The size thresholds still determine whether an entity is essential or important.

exemptions.text: Under Article 2(1), NIS2 applies to entities of a type referred to in Annex I or II that qualify as medium-sized enterprises or exceed the ceilings for medium-sized enterprises. Regardless of size, it also applies where the entity is the sole provider in a Member State of a service essential for critical societal or economic activities, where disruption of its service could have a significant impact on public safety, public security or public health or induce a significant systemic risk, or where it is critical because of its specific importance at national or regional level (Article 2(2), points (b) to (e)), and to entities identified as critical entities under Directive (EU) 2022/2557 (Article 2(3)).

rules.rationale: DORA has applied since 17 January 2025 as a Regulation, with no transposition patchwork. It governs ICT risk management, incident reporting, digital operational resilience testing and third-party risk arrangements for financial entities.

exemptions.text: Under Article 2(3), DORA does not apply to managers of alternative investment funds referred to in Article 3(2) of Directive 2011/61/EU; insurance and reinsurance undertakings referred to in Article 4 of Directive 2009/138/EC; institutions for occupational retirement provision which operate pension schemes that together have no more than 15 members in total; persons exempted under Articles 2 and 3 of Directive 2014/65/EU; insurance, reinsurance and ancillary insurance intermediaries which are microenterprises or small or medium-sized enterprises; and post office giro institutions. Under Article 2(4), a Member State may exclude entities referred to in Article 2(5), points (4) to (23), of Directive 2013/36/EU located in its territory.

Under Article 16(1), Articles 5 to 15 do not apply to small and non-interconnected investment firms, payment institutions exempted under Directive (EU) 2015/2366, institutions exempted under Directive 2013/36/EU for which the Member State has not used the option in Article 2(4), electronic money institutions exempted under Directive 2009/110/EC, and small institutions for occupational retirement provision; they must instead maintain a simplified ICT risk management framework. Under Article 24(1), microenterprises are not required to establish a digital operational resilience testing programme.

depends_on: Which category of financial entity, which determines the proportionality of the requirements.

rules.rationale: The Cyber Resilience Act sets horizontal cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements across their lifecycle. Reporting of actively exploited vulnerabilities and serious incidents begins on 11 September 2026; full application follows on 11 December 2027.

exemptions.text: Under Article 2(2) to (4), (6) and (7), the Regulation does not apply to products with digital elements to which Regulation (EU) 2017/745, (EU) 2017/746 or (EU) 2019/2144 applies, to products certified in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2018/1139, to equipment within the scope of Directive 2014/90/EU, to spare parts made available to replace identical components and manufactured to the same specifications, or to products developed or modified exclusively for national security or defence purposes or specifically designed to process classified information.

Under Article 69(2), products with digital elements placed on the market before 11 December 2027 are subject to the Regulation's requirements only if, from that date, they are substantially modified; under Article 69(3), the reporting obligations of Article 14 nevertheless apply to all of them.

depends_on: Whether the product is a product with digital elements within the Regulation's definition.
